prompt: A vendor ships a closed binary built only for x86-64. Which of these sizes cannot run it?
hint: Lesson 1. Read the additive letters, and remember which processor has no letter.

choices.text: Standard_E8as_v5
choices.why: The a is AMD, which is x86-64 like Intel; the binary runs.

choices.text: Standard_D4ds_v5, the one with a local disk
choices.why: No processor letter means Intel, and the d is only a local temporary disk.

choices.text: Standard_F2as_v6, since it has no multithreading
choices.why: Whole cores instead of threads changes the speed, not the instruction set: it is AMD, x86-64.

choices.text: Standard_D4pds_v6
choices.why: Right. The p is Arm, Cobalt 100 on v6, and an Arm processor runs only programs built for Arm.

prompt: A Standard_B2ls_v2 has 2 vCPUs, a base of 30% and holds at most 864 credits. From a full bank it runs both vCPUs at 60%. How many hours until the credits are gone?
hint: Lesson 1. Credits per minute are (base × vCPUs − CPU used × vCPUs) / 100.

prompt: The order API runs on a Standard_B2s_v2 (2 vCPUs, base 40%, holds at most 1,152). It sits at a steady 55% for a ten-hour working day and at 5% for the other fourteen hours, every day. What happens to it over a month?
hint: Lesson 1. Work out what one day spends and what one night banks.

choices.text: It is held to its base from the first busy hour, because 55% is above 40%
choices.why: Above the base it spends credits; it is held to the base only when the bank is empty.

choices.text: It runs out after a few days, because every working day is a deficit
choices.why: The day spends 18 an hour, 180 in all, and the night banks 42 an hour, 588: the balance grows.

choices.text: It is never throttled: the nights bank more than the days spend
choices.why: Right. (80 − 110) / 100 is −0.3 a minute, 180 over the day; (80 − 10) / 100 is 0.7 a minute, 588 over the night.

choices.text: It is throttled once the bank reaches its limit of 1,152
choices.why: At the limit it simply stops banking more; a full bank is the opposite of throttled.

prompt: A colleague says the F family is the one to pick when a program needs less memory than D gives it. What is true of the Fasv6 series?
hint: Lesson 1. Look at the three ratios v6 sells it at, and at what each vCPU is.

choices.text: It has 2 GiB per vCPU, half what D carries
choices.why: That is the belief the lesson asks you to drop; the l letter is what halves memory, and F comes at three ratios.

choices.text: It comes at 2, 4 and 8 GiB per vCPU, and each vCPU is a whole physical core
choices.why: Right. Fals_v6, Fas_v6 and Fams_v6; it runs without simultaneous multithreading.

choices.text: It is D with a faster clock and the same two threads per core
choices.why: The difference is the threads: F on v6 gives a core per vCPU where D on Intel shares one between two.

choices.text: It is a burstable family that banks credits below its base
choices.why: Burstable is B; F sells its processor whole all the time.

prompt: The shop's web machines are built from a managed image of its own, and a new rule requires Secure Boot on every machine. What has to change?
hint: Lesson 2. Ask which kind of image of your own Trusted Launch accepts.

choices.text: Publish it as a gallery image version that supports Trusted Launch
choices.why: Right. The gallery is Microsoft's answer for an image of your own that keeps Secure Boot.

choices.text: Add securityType: 'TrustedLaunch' to each machine's declaration and keep the managed image
choices.why: Trusted Launch does not support managed images: a machine built from one is a Standard machine.

choices.text: Capture the image again as a specialised one, so the boot is already done
choices.why: Specialised or generalised is about accounts and names; it does nothing for the boot's protection.

choices.text: Run waagent -deprovision+user again before every creation
choices.why: Deprovisioning is done once, before capture, and it cannot be undone; it has nothing to do with Secure Boot.

prompt: A Bicep file uses the virtual machine API version 2025-11-01, leaves out the security profile, and names a generation 1 image. What does the machine come out as?
hint: Lesson 2. From that API version the omission means something new, on one condition.

choices.text: Trusted Launch, because that API version always defaults to it
choices.why: It defaults to Trusted Launch only when the image, the disk and the size all support it.

choices.text: The deployment fails, because Trusted Launch needs generation 2
choices.why: Nothing fails: the fallback to Standard is silent, which is why the course writes the security type down.

choices.text: A ConfidentialVM, since the image cannot take Trusted Launch
choices.why: Confidential is a separate choice, on sizes built for it, and never a fallback.

choices.text: A Standard machine, without any error to say so
choices.why: Right. A generation 1 image cannot have Trusted Launch, and that API version then quietly falls back to Standard.

prompt: Match each way of sharing a Compute Gallery to what the other side gets.
hint: Lesson 2. Three ways, each wider than the last.

pairs.left: A role on the gallery, through Azure RBAC
pairs.right: Nothing it can list: it needs the image's id from you
A read-only gallery, for up to 30 subscriptions and 5 tenants
Public images, for every Azure customer, under a name made from your prefix

right_distractors: A copy of every version in its own subscription's gallery

prompt: When `az vm image show` returns a `plan` that is not null, the image's licence terms have to be accepted, with `az vm image terms accept`, once per ___ before any template can create a machine from it.
hint: Lesson 2. Not once per machine, and not once per region.

prompt: Put what Azure VM Image Builder does, once its image template is run, in order.
hint: Lesson 2. The same four steps a person would do by hand, framed by a build machine.
items: Create a build machine in a staging resource group whose name starts IT_
Run the customisations the template lists
Generalise the build machine
Capture it to the destination, such as a gallery
Delete the build machine
trap: Capturing before generalising is the slip: a capture taken first is of one particular machine, with its keys and its user.

prompt: A Premium SSD v2 data disk is set to 2,400 IOPS. What is the most throughput it may be given, in MB/s?
hint: Lesson 3. Throughput is capped per IOPS set, below an overall ceiling.

prompt: A P30 Premium SSD (5,000 IOPS) has on-demand bursting enabled. A batch job runs it at 9,000 IOPS for 120 seconds. Operations above the tier are billed in units of 10,000. How many units does that run bill?
hint: Lesson 3. Microsoft's own example did the same with 7,000 IOPS for 60 seconds.

prompt: Every night the shop snapshots shop-db-data and then shop-db-log, one disk at a time. What is the weakness, and what does Microsoft offer instead?
hint: Lesson 3. A snapshot covers one disk at one moment.

choices.text: Incremental snapshots cannot be restored on their own; take full ones
choices.why: The first incremental is a full copy and each later one restores; the weakness is between the two disks, not inside either.

choices.text: A snapshot is a copy in the same three places as the disk, so it is no backup; use ZRS
choices.why: A snapshot is a resource of its own, and ZRS is redundancy, which no more protects from a mistake than LRS does.

choices.text: Data and log come from two moments; a restore point takes all disks
choices.why: Right. Two snapshots of two disks are taken at two moments.

choices.text: Snapshots stop the database while they are taken; detach the disks first
choices.why: A snapshot is crash-consistent and taken while the machine carries on; nothing is stopped.

prompt: The shop's database disk must keep working through the loss of a zone, attached to a machine in another zone. Which SKU fits?
hint: Lesson 3. Read the redundancy in the SKU's name, and which types offer the zone-redundant kind.

choices.text: Premium_ZRS
choices.why: Right. Three copies in three zones, and a ZRS disk is the kind Microsoft documents attaching from another zone.

choices.text: PremiumV2_ZRS, for the separate IOPS and the zones
choices.why: There is no such SKU: zone redundancy is not offered for Premium SSD v2.

choices.text: Premium_LRS with a snapshot every hour
choices.why: An LRS disk lives in one zone; a snapshot is a way to make a new disk later, not to keep this one attached.

choices.text: UltraSSD_LRS, the fastest type
choices.why: Speed is not redundancy; it is LRS, all three copies in one datacentre.

prompt: Every one-minute sample reads 60 until 12:00 and 90 from 12:01. The rule averages a ten-minute window and fires when the average is GreaterThan 70. How many minutes after 12:00 does it first fire?
hint: Lesson 4. Each minute swaps one old sample for a new one.

prompt: Five instances are running. Two scale-out rules fire in the same run: one is ChangeCount 2, the other ExactCount 9. What count does autoscale set?
hint: Lesson 4. Rules that scale out are combined differently from rules that scale in.

choices.text: Seven, from the first rule in the list
choices.why: Order in the list decides nothing; the engine compares the counts the rules ask for.

choices.text: Nine, the larger of the two new counts
choices.why: Right. When several scale-out rules fire, the engine takes the largest new count.

choices.text: Eleven, adding both rules' changes
choices.why: The rules are not summed; each proposes a count and one of those is taken.

choices.text: Seven, the smaller change, to avoid flapping
choices.why: Fewest is the scale-in rule; scale-outs are never checked for flapping and take the largest.

prompt: Which of these needs a Uniform scale set rather than a Flexible one?
hint: Lesson 4. Microsoft's comparison names two things only the older mode supports.

choices.text: Listing two sizes and letting Azure pick the cheapest at each scale-out
choices.why: That is instance mix, and it exists only in Flexible mode.

choices.text: A Service Fabric cluster
choices.why: Right. Service Fabric and AKS are the two things the comparison lists as Uniform only.

choices.text: Attaching a virtual machine that already exists
choices.why: Only a Flexible set accepts an existing virtual machine.

choices.text: Backing up one instance with Azure Backup
choices.why: Azure Backup works on a Flexible instance, an ordinary virtual machine, and is listed as incompatible with Uniform.

prompt: Match each repairAction of automatic instance repairs to what the repaired instance keeps.
hint: Lesson 4. From most replaced to least.

pairs.right: Nothing: a new instance id, a new private address and new disks
Its address and its data disks, with a new OS disk
Everything it had

right_distractors: Its disks, moved to a healthy host in another zone

prompt: A new Flexible scale set's instances boot, and their cloud-init fails to download packages from the internet. Nothing in the network was changed. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Lesson 4. One of the differences between the modes matters on the first day.

choices.text: The instances are in a placement group of 100, which has no route out
choices.why: A placement group is about fault domains and size, not about routes.

choices.text: The health extension holds traffic back until the first probe passes
choices.why: The extension asks a local address and decides health; it does not gate the instance's outbound traffic.

choices.text: A Flexible set has no default outbound internet access
choices.why: Right. Its instances reach the internet only through something you set up.

choices.text: The upgrade policy is Manual, so the instances do not get the network profile
choices.why: Every new instance is made from the current model, network profile included, in every mode.

prompt: A Flexible scale set has baseRegularPriorityCount: 4 and regularPriorityPercentageAboveBase: 50. At a capacity of 15, how many of its instances are Spot, rounding as the documentation's worked examples do?
hint: Lesson 5. The base first; the share applies to what is above it, and the odd instance goes one way.

prompt: Which of these Spot plans cannot be built at all?
hint: Lesson 5. One of the early restrictions is about where a Spot machine may be placed.

choices.text: A Flexible scale set with two regular instances and the rest Spot
choices.why: That is Spot Priority Mix, and Flexible is the mode it needs.

choices.text: A Spot worker evicted with Delete, on an ephemeral OS disk
choices.why: The guide recommends exactly that pairing: the disk dies at every eviction anyway.

choices.text: A Spot machine with maxPrice: -1 in zone 2
choices.why: -1 is the capacity-only eviction type, and a zone is no obstacle.

choices.text: Three Spot machines placed in an availability set
choices.why: Right. Spot is not allowed in an availability set; there is an error code for exactly that.

prompt: The report machine's listener sends Metadata:true and the right api-version, but its HTTP library goes through the proxy named in the machine's HTTPS_PROXY. What is wrong?
hint: Lesson 5. Where the metadata service answers, and what the documentation says about proxies.

choices.text: Skip the proxy: the request must never leave the host
choices.why: Right. That is what --noproxy "*" does in the curl line, and an opener with no proxy in the listener.

choices.text: Nothing; any route to 169.254.169.254 reaches the same service
choices.why: The service is not meant to be reached through a proxy: the address answers only from inside the machine.

choices.text: Only the first request goes wrong, because that one switches the service on
choices.why: The first request switching it on is a separate fact; through a proxy, every request goes the wrong way.

choices.text: It must ask over HTTPS instead, which the proxy then lets through
choices.why: The documented request is plain http to that address; the fix is to skip the proxy, not to change the scheme.

prompt: Match each Scheduled Events type to its documented minimum notice.
hint: Lesson 5. One of them is the Spot eviction.

pairs.right: 15 minutes
10 minutes
30 seconds, best effort
5 to 15 minutes, configured on the scale set

prompt: Which of these belong on Spot? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 5. Ask what one eviction costs each of them.

choices.text: CI build agents for the shop's pull requests
choices.why: Right. An interrupted build runs again, and builds are made to be repeatable.

choices.text: The shop's only database server
choices.why: A single machine holding state is the first thing the lesson keeps off Spot.

choices.text: Queue workers above a floor of regular ones
choices.why: Right. A job not completed comes back, so an eviction costs one job done twice.

choices.text: The three machines the order API needs to answer at all
choices.why: The minimum a service needs to stay up is the regular base; only what is above it goes on Spot.

choices.text: A batch job that writes a checkpoint every half hour
choices.why: Right. An eviction costs the minutes since the last checkpoint.

prompt: A single machine has a Premium SSD OS disk and one data disk on Standard SSD. Over the agreement's 30 days, how many minutes of downtime does its promise allow?
hint: Lesson 6. A machine with mixed disks is promised what its weakest disk is.

prompt: To save money, the team creates shop-web-1 in the set, stops and deallocates it, and then creates shop-web-2 in the same set. What is the risk?
hint: Lesson 6. The documentation describes this exact sequence.

choices.text: shop-web-2 is refused, because a set needs every machine running
choices.why: Nothing is refused; the sequence works and leaves the placement weaker.

choices.text: shop-web-2's disk is free to land in shop-web-1's fault domain
choices.why: Right. The documented advice is to leave the first running until the second exists.

choices.text: shop-web-1 loses its place in the set when it is deallocated
choices.why: A machine joins a set at creation and stays in it; deallocating does not remove it.

choices.text: The two machines are put in the same update domain for ever
choices.why: Update domains wrap from the sixth machine; the second takes a different one whatever the first is doing.

prompt: A zone-spanning scale set uses Strict zone balancing. Zone 3 goes dark, and autoscale asks for two more instances. What happens?
hint: Lesson 6. The two balancing modes answer an outage differently.

choices.text: The scale-out is blocked, because it would leave the set unbalanced
choices.why: Right. Strict blocks an unbalancing operation even while a zone is down.

choices.text: They go to zones 1 and 2, and are moved to zone 3 once it is back
choices.why: Best effort would place them in the working zones, and nothing ever moves an instance afterwards.

choices.text: They wait in zone 3's queue and start there when it returns
choices.why: There is no queue per zone; the operation is blocked.

choices.text: They are created as regional instances, outside any zone
choices.why: Every instance of a zone-spanning set is zonal; it never makes a regional one.

prompt: Match each arrangement to the uptime the agreement read on 2026-10-30 promises it.
hint: Lesson 6. Each nine is a different size of failure survived.

pairs.left: One machine, all disks Premium SSD
Two or more machines in one availability set
Two or more machines across two or more zones

prompt: A resource that keeps the machines named in it physically close, pinned to one datacentre for the lowest latency between them, is a proximity ___ group.
hint: Lesson 6. It trades the protection of distance for speed.

prompt: A container group runs a payment batch that must never run twice once it has succeeded. Its policy is Never. What else does the job need, by Microsoft's documentation?
hint: Lesson 7. Read the note the documentation attaches to Never.

choices.text: Nothing; Never means the container is not started again in any case
choices.why: After a non-zero exit the platform may still restart it, so Never alone is not at most once.

choices.text: A retry cap of zero, written as OnFailure:0
choices.why: The cap is Docker's own syntax; Container Instances documents no retry cap at all.

choices.text: To run in a virtual network, where restarts are switched off
choices.why: Where a group is reached from has nothing to do with whether it is restarted.

choices.text: To catch its own failures and always exit 0
choices.why: Right. A job that must run at most once has to make sure it never exits with an error code.

prompt: The report's group runs in a subnet delegated to Container Instances and has to call a supplier's API on the internet. What gives it the way out?
hint: Lesson 7. Microsoft names one supported way.

choices.text: A public IP address added to the group beside its private one
choices.why: A group in a virtual network has no public address, and the CLI refuses to give it one.

choices.text: A DNS label, which makes the group reachable in both directions
choices.why: A DNS label is for a public group, and a group in a subnet cannot have one.

choices.text: A NAT gateway on the subnet
choices.why: Right. The documentation calls it the only supported way out for a group in a virtual network.

choices.text: A sidecar container in the group that forwards the traffic out
choices.why: A sidecar shares the group's network and has no way out the group lacks.

prompt: Which of these can be changed on an existing container group only by deleting it and creating it again? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 7. An update is the create run again with the same name; a few properties do not move that way.

choices.text: The restart policy
choices.why: Right. It is one of the properties fixed for the life of the group.

choices.text: The CPU and memory requests
choices.why: Right. The size is fixed: changing it means a new group.

choices.text: The image tag of a container
choices.why: A new image is the ordinary update: the create again, and the containers restart in place.

choices.text: The network profile
choices.why: Right. Moving a group into or out of a virtual network means recreating it.

choices.text: The availability zone
choices.why: Right. The zone is on the documented list as well.

prompt: How does a Spot container group differ from lesson 5's Spot virtual machine when capacity is taken back?
hint: Lesson 7. Look for the setting the container version does not have.

choices.text: It is deleted with its volumes, as Delete would do on a machine
choices.why: Nothing is chosen and nothing is deleted for good; Azure restarts the group.

choices.text: It is moved to a regular host, keeping its public address
choices.why: A Spot group has no public address to keep in the first place.

choices.text: There is no eviction policy to choose: Azure restarts the evicted group on its own
choices.why: Right. The container version has no Deallocate or Delete; the group comes back by itself.

choices.text: It waits deallocated until somebody starts it, as Deallocate would
choices.why: That is the machine's default; the container group does not wait for anybody.

prompt: A queue rule asks for one replica per 10 messages, with maxReplicas 30. One replica is running when 200 messages arrive. Following the documentation's step formula, what count does the third scaling step reach?
hint: Lesson 8. Each step is min(maxReplicaCount, desiredReplicas, max(4, 2 × currentReplicaCount)).

prompt: The shop wants session affinity for its order API and a 90/10 canary for its next release, both at once. What does the documentation allow?
hint: Lesson 8. Each of the two needs a revision mode.

choices.text: Not both: affinity needs single mode, and a weighted split needs multiple
choices.why: Right. Single keeps one active revision, so there is nothing to split.

choices.text: Both, as long as the canary's revision carries a label
choices.why: A label gives a revision an address; it does not change which mode affinity needs.

choices.text: Both, because affinity pins each client to one revision of the split
choices.why: Affinity sends a client to the same replica by a cookie, and it is supported only in single mode.

choices.text: Both, in the preview Labels mode, which combines the two
choices.why: The course does not rely on the Labels mode, and nothing it read says it brings affinity.

prompt: Match each change to the shop's container app with what it does.
hint: Lesson 8. The split between template and configuration decides most of them.

pairs.right: Creates a new revision
Applies to every revision, and creates none

pairs.left: A new value for the registry secret
pairs.right: Is not seen by a running revision until it restarts
Cannot be changed once the environment exists

right_distractors: Restarts every replica in place, as a container group update would

prompt: In a workload profiles environment, scale to zero belongs to the ___ profile, the one every such environment comes with and cannot remove.
hint: Lesson 8. Not Dedicated, and not the Flexible preview.

prompt: In single revision mode, put a deployment of a new revision of the shop in order.
hint: Lesson 8. Traffic moves last, and only once.
items: The new revision is created beside the old one
It is scaled up to the old revision's replica count, within its own limits
Every replica passes its startup and readiness probes
All the traffic moves to the new revision
The old revision is deprovisioned
trap: Moving the traffic before the probes pass is the slip: it is the waiting that leaves the traffic on the old revision when the new one never becomes ready.

prompt: Two replicas of the shop save order-1 through Dapr's state store at almost the same moment, neither sending an ETag. What happens?
hint: Lesson 9. The guard against two writers works only when it is asked for.

choices.text: The second write is refused with 409
choices.why: 409 is the answer to a write carrying a stale ETag; a write with none is never refused.

choices.text: The first one wins, because Dapr's stores are first-write-wins
choices.why: First-write-wins is what an ETag buys; it is not the default.

choices.text: Each replica gets its own copy under its own key
choices.why: The key prefix is the app id, and both replicas share the app id shop.

choices.text: Both succeed and the last one wins
choices.why: Right. Without an ETag the default is last-write-wins, and the documentation tells you to assume it.

prompt: The nightly report is moved to a Container Apps job, and the team wants it to publish its result through the environment's Dapr pub/sub component. What does Microsoft's documentation say?
hint: Lesson 9. One of the things Container Apps leaves out of Dapr is about jobs.

choices.text: It works once the component's scopes list the job's name
choices.why: Scopes narrow which app ids load a component; they cannot give Dapr to something that has none.

choices.text: A Container Apps job cannot have Dapr
choices.why: Right. Dapr is for container apps; the report would publish with the broker's own library.

choices.text: It works only with a Tier 1 component
choices.why: The tiers say which components are supported; the obstacle here is the job.

choices.text: It works if the job runs Dapr's own configuration file
choices.why: Dapr's own configuration file cannot be used in Container Apps at all.

prompt: The order API will only ever talk to one Service Bus namespace, and it needs Service Bus sessions. Why is Dapr a poor fit for it?
hint: Lesson 9. Ask what the building block does not name, and where it is reached if at all.

choices.text: What the building block lacks ties the code back to one broker
choices.why: Right. It pays the process and the hop and gives up direct use of the broker; the broker's own library serves it better.

choices.text: Dapr cannot reach a real Service Bus namespace, only the emulator
choices.why: The same component signs in to a real namespace, with a managed identity in Container Apps.

choices.text: Sessions need a second sidecar per replica
choices.why: One sidecar serves every building block; the number of sidecars is not the issue.

choices.text: Dapr forbids pub/sub on a queue and requires a topic
choices.why: Dapr has a component for Service Bus queues; it was the one swapped in.

prompt: Match each answer a subscriber gives to a delivery with what the sidecar does next.
hint: Lesson 9. Three are words in the reply's body; one is a status code.

pairs.right: The message is done with
The message is delivered again
The message is discarded
The message is dropped with an error in the sidecar's log

right_distractors: The message is moved to a dead-letter queue by Dapr

prompt: A task builds the shop from a two-stage Dockerfile: a build stage FROM one image and a final stage FROM python:3.12-slim. The build stage's base image is patched under its same tag. Does the base image trigger rebuild the shop?
hint: Lesson 10. Which base the documentation says a task tracks.

choices.text: Yes, within 10 to 60 minutes, as for any base on a public registry
choices.why: That delay is real for a public base, but this base is not tracked at all.

choices.text: Yes, at once, because both stages are in the same Dockerfile
choices.why: Being in the same file is not what the trigger reads; it records the final image's base.

choices.text: No: only the final image's base is tracked
choices.why: Right. The stages before it in a multi-stage Dockerfile are not followed.

choices.text: Only if the pull request trigger is switched on
choices.why: The pull request trigger is about pull requests; base images have their own trigger.

prompt: Defender for Cloud's plan for containers is on for the subscription. Which of the shop's images does it stop scanning?
hint: Lesson 10. It scans what is pushed or imported, and what has been pulled recently.

choices.text: 1.2, pushed this morning and not yet pulled
choices.why: A push is one of the events that gets an image scanned.

choices.text: 1.0, pushed in January and pulled by nobody for 45 days
choices.why: Right. It was scanned when pushed, and drops out once 30 days pass with no pull.

choices.text: 1.1, pulled by the cluster's nodes every day
choices.why: An image pulled in the last 30 days stays scanned.

choices.text: python:3.12-slim, kept in the registry by an artifact cache rule
choices.why: A cached image is pulled through the registry, and the rule fetched it when somebody pulled it.

prompt: A weekly task runs acr purge --filter 'shop:.*' --ago 30d --untagged. Release 1.1 was pushed 40 days ago and still runs in production. What keeps it in the registry?
hint: Lesson 10. The filter matches release tags as well.

choices.text: Its tag: purge deletes only manifests left without one
choices.why: --ago 30d removes tags older than thirty days first, release tags included.

choices.text: The deployment pulling it by digest
choices.why: Pulling by digest protects against a moved tag, not against a deletion: the warnings say not to purge what something pulls by digest.

choices.text: Nothing; a purge cannot be told to keep anything
choices.why: A lock is exactly how a purge is told to keep something.

choices.text: Locking it: az acr repository update --image shop:1.1 --write-enabled false
choices.why: Right. Purge skips a locked tag, which is what the tagging guidance recommends for what is deployed.

prompt: A token handed to `az acr build` as a build argument is visible to the ACR team, so it goes in the option `--___-build-arg` instead, which is kept out of what they see.
hint: Lesson 10. One word in front of build-arg.

prompt: The shop starts on a Basic registry. Which of these does it already have there? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 10. The tiers speak one API; the features differ.

choices.text: The same push and pull API as Premium
choices.why: Right. A pipeline written against Basic works unchanged against Premium.

choices.text: A replica in southcentralus
choices.why: Geo-replication is Premium only.

choices.text: An artifact cache rule for python:3.12-slim
choices.why: Right. Artifact cache is in all three tiers.

choices.text: Zone redundancy across the region's zones
choices.why: Right. On by default in every tier, in a region with zones, whatever the property says.

choices.text: A private endpoint
choices.why: Private endpoints are Premium only.

prompt: A cluster was left on a minor version past its end of life for more than sixty days, with a Sunday maintenance window and a budget of three of three on the shop. What does AKS do?
hint: Lesson 11. The documentation names this kind of upgrade, and says what it ignores.

choices.text: Nothing until somebody runs az aks upgrade, since upgradeChannel decides
choices.why: Past sixty days after end of life AKS acts whatever the channel says.

choices.text: It upgrades the cluster on the next Sunday, stopping at the blocked drain
choices.why: A platform-initiated upgrade does not wait for the window, and it does not stop at the budget.

choices.text: It moves the cluster to the Premium tier's long-term support
choices.why: Long-term support is never automatic: it needs the Premium tier and the plan chosen explicitly.

choices.text: AKS acts by itself, one minor at a time, and overrides both
choices.why: Right. That is the platform-initiated upgrade, which brings the cluster back to a supported version.

prompt: The shop upgraded its control plane and then the pool apps to 1.37, and the shop now misbehaves. Five days have passed. What can be undone?
hint: Lesson 11. The two halves of an upgrade go back differently, if at all.

choices.text: Both, with az aks upgrade --kubernetes-version 1.36
choices.why: A control plane upgrade cannot be rolled back.

choices.text: Neither: an AKS upgrade is final
choices.why: A node pool can go back, within limits.

choices.text: The pool apps, one version back, for seven days
choices.why: Right. From API version 2026-04-01; the control plane stays on 1.37.

choices.text: The control plane alone, since the pools may lag it by three versions
choices.why: The lag lets you upgrade the control plane first; it does not let you take it back.

prompt: A cluster runs 1.36.2; 1.36.6, 1.37.1 and 1.37.3 are available, and 1.37 is the newest minor. Match each upgradeChannel to where it takes the Kubernetes version.
hint: Lesson 11. Each channel names a minor version and then takes its latest patch.

pairs.right: Stays on 1.36.2

prompt: A Standard cluster without availability zones has an uptime SLA of 99.9% on its API server. Over a month of 730 hours, how many minutes may it be unreachable without breaking the promise?
hint: Lesson 11. The same arithmetic as lesson 6, over 730 hours.

prompt: A cluster outside long-term support runs 1.35 on its control plane and every pool, and has to reach 1.37. Put the upgrades in order.
hint: Lesson 11. No minor version is skipped, and the pools follow the control plane, never lead it.
items: The control plane to 1.36
The pools to 1.36
The control plane to 1.37
The pools to 1.37
trap: Moving the pools first is the slip: a node pool may lag the control plane, and may never run ahead of it.

prompt: A pod carries karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true" on a node whose NodePool sets expireAfter, and the node reaches that age. What happens?
hint: Lesson 12. Of the three ways nodes go away, one is the forceful one.

choices.text: The node is replaced anyway: expiry ignores the annotation and the budgets
choices.why: Right. That is why the lesson's pool turned expiry off and left the budgets in charge.

choices.text: Nothing, until the pod finishes, because the annotation holds every disruption
choices.why: The annotation holds off consolidation and drift, and not expiry.

choices.text: The node waits for the pool's budget to allow it
choices.why: Expiry is the one disruption the budgets cannot hold back.

choices.text: The pod is moved to a system node, which never expires
choices.why: No pod of yours may run on a managed system node, even with a broad toleration.

prompt: The shop writes a NodePool budget of 0 for 09:00 to 21:00, meaning São Paulo's selling hours, three hours behind UTC. When does it actually close disruptions?
hint: Lesson 12. There is a field to fix this in lesson 11's windows, and none here.

choices.text: From 09:00 to 21:00 in São Paulo, taken from the cluster's region
choices.why: Nothing reads the region; a budget's schedule is in UTC and cannot be anything else.

choices.text: From 06:00 to 18:00 in São Paulo, because the schedule is in UTC
choices.why: Right. Three hours early, so the shop's evening is open to consolidation.

choices.text: From 12:00 to 24:00 in São Paulo, because Karpenter adds the offset
choices.why: The offset goes the other way, and Karpenter adds none: it reads the schedule as UTC.

choices.text: Never: a budget of 0 is refused by the CRD
choices.why: 0 is a valid budget, and the most restrictive active budget wins.

prompt: A NodePool owns 15 nodes and has one budget of "25%". One node is already being deleted and one is not ready. How many more nodes may Karpenter disrupt now?
hint: Lesson 12. The node count times the percentage, rounded up, minus what is already going and what is not ready.

prompt: On an Automatic cluster, a container's manifest requests 50m of CPU and 64Mi of memory. What does the resource requests safeguard do?
hint: Lesson 12. The mutator has values for nothing written, and a floor for something too small.

choices.text: Raises them to the minimum of 100m and 100Mi
choices.why: Right. A small value is raised to 100m of CPU and 100Mi of memory.

choices.text: Refuses the pod, because the requests are below the minimum
choices.why: Requests are a rule that mutates; it is probes and latest that only refuse.

choices.text: Replaces both with 500m and 2048Mi
choices.why: Those are the values for a container with no requests and no limits at all.

choices.text: Leaves them, since any written request is accepted
choices.why: A value that is given but small is raised to the minimum.

prompt: On an Automatic cluster, the nightly report's pod asks for more than any running node has free. Put what happens in order.
hint: Lesson 12. The pod's requests are where the size comes from.
items: The scheduler finds no node and leaves the pod Pending
NAP reads the pod's requests and keeps the sizes its NodePools allow that would hold it
NAP creates a machine, and a NodeClaim records what it asked Azure for
The pod is scheduled on the new node
The report finishes, and consolidation removes the empty node
trap: Creating the machine before reading the requests is the slip: NAP starts from the pending pod, which is the opposite end from a pool with a fixed size.

prompt: The shop rotates its cluster's signing keys with az aks oidc-issuer rotate-signing-keys. Why do the old key and the new one both stay valid for 24 hours?
hint: Lesson 13. Think about the tokens already sitting in pods' files.

choices.text: Because Entra ID refetches an issuer's keys only once a day
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson gives Entra ID's refresh interval; the overlap is about the tokens in the pods.

choices.text: Because the federated credentials must be edited to name the new key
choices.why: A credential names an issuer, a subject and an audience; it never names a key.

choices.text: So every pod's token is replaced before the old key stops counting
choices.why: Right. A projected token lasts an hour by default, so a day covers every replacement.

choices.text: Because the issuer's address changes and the old one must keep answering
choices.why: The issuer's address carries a GUID that never changes; only the keys behind it rotate.

prompt: A pod's script asks Entra ID's token endpoint for a token with scope=https://storage.azure.com/, as it did on a virtual machine through the metadata service. What does the documentation warn?
hint: Lesson 13. The two flows use different endpoints, and they want the resource written differently.

choices.text: Nothing: the endpoint accepts the resource in either form
choices.why: The bare form can fail here; that is exactly the warning.

choices.text: The scope is ignored and the token is for every resource the identity may reach
choices.why: A token is for the one resource the request named; nothing widens it.

choices.text: It fails with AADSTS700212, because the audience is wrong
choices.why: That code is for a token whose audience is not the credential's, a different mistake.

choices.text: Version 2 wants <resource>/.default, which the bare form lacks
choices.why: Right. The metadata service took the bare resource; the v2 endpoint wants <resource>/.default.

prompt: Five minutes after shop-orders was given Storage Blob Data Contributor on the receipts container, the pod gets an access token from Entra ID and the storage account refuses its write. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: Lesson 13. The token was issued, so the exchange worked.

choices.text: The federated credential has not propagated yet
choices.why: A credential that had not propagated would have stopped the token being issued at all.

choices.text: The new role has not taken effect yet
choices.why: Right. A pod refused just after setup has usually been set up correctly and too recently.

choices.text: The projected token expired before the write
choices.why: The access token was issued; what the storage account checks is the identity's role.

choices.text: The role must be given to the kubelet identity as well
choices.why: That would give every pod on the node the role; the pod acts as shop-orders alone.

prompt: A team tries to add the federated credential to a system-assigned identity, to avoid creating a resource of its own. What does the lesson say?
hint: Lesson 13. Which two kinds of identity a federated credential can sit on.

choices.text: Not there: user-assigned or an app registration only
choices.why: Right. A system-assigned identity lives and dies with one resource.

choices.text: It works, and the credential is deleted with the cluster
choices.why: A credential is a child of the identity and is never deleted with a cluster.

choices.text: It works, but only for the kubelet's own pods
choices.why: The kubelet identity is a node's, and it is the route the lesson warns against.

choices.text: It works once the OIDC issuer is turned on
choices.why: The issuer is needed either way; it does not change which identities take a credential.

prompt: Behind AGIC, the shop scales in from five pods to three and some customers get a 502 for a minute. Why, and what does the documentation recommend?
hint: Lesson 14. The change travels a long road before the gateway knows about it.

choices.text: The AGIC pod was busy and dropped the requests passing through it; give it more replicas
choices.why: AGIC carries no requests at all: the gateway sends them straight to the pods.

choices.text: kube-proxy was still routing to the old pods; switch to a NodePort
choices.why: There is no kube-proxy on the way: the gateway talks to pod addresses directly.

choices.text: The health probe used the Ingress path /, which answers 404
choices.why: That would make every pod unhealthy all the time, not for a minute during a scale-in.

choices.text: Pods that had gone still got requests until ARM updated the gateway
choices.why: Right. The gateway might take a minute to get an update, and draining is the documented answer.

prompt: An Application Gateway already serves the company's website, and the team wants AGIC to add the shop's rules to it without touching the rest. How must AGIC be installed?
hint: Lesson 14. By default AGIC owns its gateway outright.

choices.text: As the AKS add-on, with --appgw-id pointing at that gateway
choices.why: The add-on takes full ownership and would delete the hand-made listeners; shared mode is not offered there.

choices.text: As the add-on, with --appgw-subnet-cidr, so it gets a subnet of its own
choices.why: That creates a new gateway in the node resource group; it does not share the existing one.

choices.text: With Helm, in shared mode
choices.why: Right. Shared mode, and ProhibitedTargets with it, are only in the Helm installation.

choices.text: Any way, as long as the gateway is on the WAF_v2 SKU
choices.why: WAF_v2 is one of the two SKUs AGIC works with; it says nothing about sharing.

prompt: A rule of an HTTPRoute lists three backends with weights 2, 2 and 1. What percentage of the rule's requests goes to the third?
hint: Lesson 14. A weight is a proportion of the sum in its list.

prompt: The finance export wants an entry point through Application Gateway for Containers that is reachable only from the virtual network, on port 8443. What does the documentation say?
hint: Lesson 14. Read what a frontend listens on, and what kind of address it has.

choices.text: It works with a second association in the finance subnet
choices.why: Today a resource can have only one association, and an association is not a frontend anyway.

choices.text: A frontend listens on ports 80 and 443 only and has no private address
choices.why: Right. Neither half of that request fits what a frontend is.

choices.text: It works with the ALB Controller managing the frontend
choices.why: Who manages a frontend changes who owns it, not what it can listen on.

choices.text: It works if a ReferenceGrant in finance allows it
choices.why: A grant permits a reference across namespaces; it has nothing to do with ports or addresses.

prompt: Behind Application Gateway for Containers, the shop's /report endpoint takes about 90 seconds to answer, and the route sets no timeouts. What do callers get?
hint: Lesson 14. The data plane has a default wait.

choices.text: The answer, since the data plane waits as long as the pod does
choices.why: It waits 60 seconds unless the route says otherwise.

choices.text: A timeout: the data plane waits 60 seconds unless told
choices.why: Right. timeouts.request on the route is where a longer wait is written.

choices.text: The answer, after the connection-draining timeout of 30 seconds is added
choices.why: Connection draining is an AGIC annotation for pods being removed, not a request timeout.

choices.text: A 500, as for a backend that does not exist
choices.why: The 500 is what the specification asks for an invalid backend; this one exists and is slow.

prompt: A blob output's path is '%RECEIPTS%/{order}.json'. The app's setting RECEIPTS is receipts-2026, and the queue message is {"order": "A-3003", "sku": "cap", "qty": 1}. Which blob does a successful run write?
hint: Lesson 15. Two kinds of binding expression, read from two different places.

choices.text: %RECEIPTS%/A-3003.json, since only braces are expressions
choices.why: Percent signs are expressions too, read from a setting.

choices.text: receipts-2026/cap.json
choices.why: {order} reads the order field of the message, not the sku.

choices.text: receipts-2026/A-3003.json
choices.why: Right. %RECEIPTS% comes from the setting and {order} from the JSON message that triggered the run.

choices.text: None: the host cannot read a field of a base64-encoded message
choices.why: The host decodes its own base64 messages; it is a sender outside the binding that has to encode.

prompt: make_receipt also has to write to storage in a way its blob output binding cannot express. How does it do that?
hint: Lesson 15. What the documentation says about the clients behind a binding.

choices.text: With the Azure SDK, a client the function creates and configures itself
choices.why: Right. A binding offers what its extension offers and nothing more.

choices.text: It borrows the binding's own storage client through the receipt parameter
choices.why: The code cannot access the underlying clients used by the binding extensions.

choices.text: With a second blob output on the same path, which adds the missing options
choices.why: A second binding offers the same options as the first.

choices.text: By setting the missing options in host.json under extensions.blobs
choices.why: host.json tunes how the extension behaves; it cannot make a binding do a kind of write it does not have.

prompt: With managed identities, match each connection of the shop's app to the role the documentation's table gives it.
hint: Lesson 15. Roles are granted per binding.

pairs.right: Storage Blob Data Owner
Storage Queue Data Reader with Storage Queue Data Message Processor
Storage Queue Data Contributor

prompt: A function has exactly ___ trigger, and any number of input and output bindings.
hint: Lesson 15. The trigger is the binding that also starts the function.

prompt: The nightly finance export is a timer-triggered function on a Dedicated plan, beside a web app, with Always On off. Nobody calls the function app over HTTP. What happens at night?
hint: Lesson 16. What wakes an idle runtime on that plan.

choices.text: It runs on time, because a Dedicated plan is billed whether or not it works
choices.why: Paying for the plan does not keep the runtime awake; Always On does.

choices.text: It runs late, after a cold start of a few seconds
choices.why: Nothing starts it at all: only an HTTP request wakes an idle runtime there.

choices.text: It runs on a prewarmed instance kept for scale-out
choices.why: Prewarmed instances are a Premium plan's buffer, not a Dedicated one's.

choices.text: A timer that nothing wakes: only HTTP wakes an idle runtime
choices.why: Right. A timer trigger silently not running is the documented consequence.

prompt: On Flex Consumption, the minimum billable execution period is 1,000 ms, rounded up to the nearest 100 ms after that. An execution lasts 1,340 ms. How many milliseconds are billed?
hint: Lesson 16. Past the minimum, the rounding is up.

prompt: A Flex Consumption app has zone redundancy switched on, and always ready set to one instance for the http group. What does the documentation require?
hint: Lesson 16. Zone redundancy puts a floor under the count.

choices.text: Nothing more; one always ready instance is spread across zones by itself
choices.why: An instance runs in one place; the documentation asks for more than one.

choices.text: Always ready instances for every function group, not only http
choices.why: The requirement is per group that has them, and it is about the count.

choices.text: A move to Premium, since Flex has no zone redundancy
choices.why: Flex has zone redundancy; it comes with this condition.

choices.text: At least two always ready instances per group
choices.why: Right. With zone redundancy on, the documentation requires at least two.

prompt: All the Flex Consumption apps of a subscription share a regional quota of 250 cores by default. If every instance is the 4,096 MB size, which has two cores, how many instances can run in that region at once?
hint: Lesson 16. Memory and processor come together in each size.

prompt: Whatever a function app's timeout says, an HTTP function has ___ seconds to answer, the idle timeout of the load balancer in front of the app.
hint: Lesson 16. Longer work goes to a queue or to Durable Functions.

prompt: An orchestrator calls five activities one after another, each behind its own yield, and then returns. On the Azure Storage provider every run of the orchestrator adds four events to the History table. How many events does the order's history hold at the end, leaving out the sentinel row?
hint: Lesson 17. Count the runs first: one per activity result, plus the first.

prompt: A bug in the bank's webhook raises PaymentConfirmed for instance A-2001-X instead of A-2001. What does the management API do, and what does that mean for the shop?
hint: Lesson 17. The documentation says what happens to an event for an id that does not exist.

choices.text: It answers 410 Gone, which the webhook logs as an error
choices.why: 410 is for an instance that has completed or failed, not one that never existed.

choices.text: It discards the event without an error, so A-2001 waits until its timer expires the order
choices.why: Right. It is the case to watch for when the id comes from a webhook: nothing complains.

choices.text: It starts a new instance called A-2001-X to hold the event
choices.why: Raising an event never starts an instance; only the client function's start_new does.

choices.text: It delivers the event to the nearest matching id, A-2001
choices.why: Ids are matched exactly; nothing guesses.

prompt: On the Consumption plan, an order goes through three sequential activities. What is billed for its orchestrator?
hint: Lesson 17. Replays, and the time spent waiting at a yield.

choices.text: One execution, lasting from the start to the last result
choices.why: The orchestrator does not run for that time; it runs four times, briefly.

choices.text: Four executions, plus the seconds it waited for each activity
choices.why: The time an orchestrator spends waiting at a yield is not billed at all.

choices.text: Four executions, one per run, and nothing for the waiting
choices.why: Right. On Consumption each replay is billed as an execution.

choices.text: Nothing; only activities are billed
choices.why: On Consumption the replays are billed; the other plans do not charge for them.

prompt: The shop's app has scaled out to 30 instances on the Azure Storage provider, with the partition count at its maximum. How many of them can run orchestrators at once?
hint: Lesson 17. An orchestrator runs on the host holding the lease on its control queue.

choices.text: At most 16
choices.why: Right. The provider has at most sixteen partitions, so at most sixteen instances hold one.

choices.text: All 30, since every instance competes for the work-item queue
choices.why: That is how activities spread; orchestrators are tied to control queues.

choices.text: 4, the default number of control queues
choices.why: Four is the default; the question set the partitions to their maximum.

choices.text: 1, because an orchestrator runs on one thread
choices.why: One thread per instance of the host, and several hosts can each hold partitions.

prompt: Which of these may order_flow, an orchestrator, do safely? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 17. It must make the same requests in the same order every time it runs.

choices.text: Read the time from context.current_utc_datetime
choices.why: Right. It comes from the history, so every replay reads the same value.

choices.text: Call datetime.now() to decide whether to ship today
choices.why: The machine's clock answers differently on each replay.

choices.text: Make an id with context.new_guid()
choices.why: Right. That is the replay-safe way to get one.

choices.text: Wait with time.sleep(60) before charging
choices.why: A wait in an orchestrator is a durable timer, never a sleep.

choices.text: Wait with yield context.create_timer(when)
choices.why: Right. That is the orchestrator's sleep, and the only one it may use.

prompt: The shop wants its existing P1v3 plan of two instances to be zone redundant, and the plan reports a maximumNumberOfZones of 1. What does the documentation leave as the way?
hint: Lesson 18. That number depends on where the plan was placed, not on its tier.

choices.text: Set zoneRedundant: true and add a third instance
choices.why: Two instances already meet the instance condition; the plan's zone count is the obstacle.

choices.text: Create the plan again, in a new resource group
choices.why: Right. A plan that answers one has to be made again, in a new resource group.

choices.text: Move the plan to Isolated v2, which is zone redundant by default
choices.why: Nothing the lesson read says a tier changes the scale unit the plan sits on.

choices.text: Nothing: Brazil South has no availability zones
choices.why: Brazil South has zones, lesson 6; the limit is this plan's scale unit.

prompt: Traffic routing sends 10% of production's visitors to staging. A customer lands on staging, and staging is then fixed and the routing set back to zero. What can that customer see?
hint: Lesson 18. How the choice of slot is remembered.

choices.text: Production on the next page, since each request is routed afresh
choices.why: The choice is kept, so a customer does not alternate between versions on every page.

choices.text: Staging for ever, until the browser's cookies are cleared
choices.why: The cookie lasts an hour, not for ever.

choices.text: The same slot for up to an hour, until its cookie runs out
choices.why: Right. The cookie holds the choice for an hour; a link with x-ms-routing-name=self names production.

choices.text: An error, because staging's address is closed to customers
choices.why: Traffic routing serves staging at production's address; an IP rule on the slot is a separate thing.

prompt: The shop's plan has two instances with healthCheckPath set. A bad configuration makes both of them fail the check. What does App Service do?
hint: Lesson 18. The health check never takes out more than a share of the instances.

choices.text: Takes neither out, and both keep receiving traffic
choices.why: Right. With every instance failing, none is taken out of the load balancer.

choices.text: Takes both out of the load balancer, so the shop answers nothing
choices.why: With every instance failing, none is taken out.

choices.text: Takes one out, the first to fail ten requests
choices.why: That would be half, the default ceiling; but with every instance failing, the documentation says none is taken out.

choices.text: Swaps staging back into production
choices.why: The health check removes and replaces instances; it never swaps slots.

prompt: The admin site shares the shop's plan, with alwaysOn off. The developers open it each morning after a quiet night. What do they notice?
hint: Lesson 18. What happens to an app that nobody calls for a while.

choices.text: Nothing: the plan's instances run all night, so the app is loaded
choices.why: The instances run, but the app on them is unloaded without Always On.

choices.text: A 503 until they swap the site from staging
choices.why: An unloaded app is loaded again by the next request; nothing has to be swapped.

choices.text: A lower bill for the night, since an unloaded app is not charged
choices.why: The plan is paid for whatever runs on it; unloading saves nothing.

choices.text: A slow first request, after 20 minutes unloaded
choices.why: Right. The next caller pays for its warm-up.

prompt: A copy of the morning export's Recurrence trigger has no timeZone, a startTime of 2026-11-02T06:00:00Z and the schedule at hour 6. When does it fire, in São Paulo, three hours behind UTC?
hint: Lesson 19. Without a zone, the trigger reads its times as one particular zone.

choices.text: At 06:00, because the region brazilsouth decides the zone
choices.why: Nothing reads the region; without timeZone the times are UTC.

choices.text: At 09:00, because UTC is three hours ahead
choices.why: Six in UTC is three in São Paulo, not nine.

choices.text: At 03:00, because the times are now UTC
choices.why: Right. Six in the morning in São Paulo would be written as 09:00:00Z.

choices.text: Never, because a Recurrence trigger needs a time zone
choices.why: The zone is optional; without it the trigger runs on UTC.

prompt: A Consumption workflow with a Recurrence trigger and no startTime is deployed disabled at 15:00 and enabled at 15:20. When is its first run?
hint: Lesson 19. This is why the lesson's file carries a startTime.

choices.text: At the next scheduled hour after 15:20
choices.why: Without a startTime it does not wait for the schedule.

choices.text: At 15:20, the moment it is enabled
choices.why: Right. A Recurrence trigger with no startTime fires as soon as the workflow is enabled.

choices.text: Never, until somebody resubmits a run
choices.why: Resubmitting reruns a finished run; it is not how a trigger starts.

choices.text: At 15:00, catching up the run it missed while disabled
choices.why: A disabled workflow runs nothing, and nothing is caught up.

prompt: One morning the export's trigger fires, Get_orders fails twice and succeeds on its third try, and Any_orders, Export, Summary and Send_export each run once. How many executions does that Consumption run bill?
hint: Lesson 19. Every try of an action is an execution, and so is the trigger.

prompt: A definition builds the shop's address as "@parameters('shopUrl')/orders". What does the documentation say?
hint: Lesson 19. Text around an expression.

choices.text: Incorrect: with text around it, the expression needs braces
choices.why: Right. @{...} puts the value inside a string.

choices.text: It is correct: the @ makes the whole string an expression
choices.why: With text around it the expression needs braces; this form is marked incorrect.

choices.text: It is correct only if shopUrl is declared as a string parameter
choices.why: The parameter's type is not the problem; the missing braces are.

choices.text: The Bicep compiler refuses it with a warning
choices.why: The compiler reads nothing inside the definition; it would pass in silence.

prompt: Get_orders fails on every retry one morning. An action Alert names Get_orders in its runAfter with Failed and TimedOut. Put what the engine does in order.
hint: Lesson 19. An action waits for the status of what it names.
items: The trigger fires at 06:00
Get_orders is tried, then retried a minute apart
Get_orders is marked Failed
Alert runs, because it named the status Failed
trap: Running Alert before Get_orders has a final status is the slip: an action waits until what it names in runAfter has finished.

prompt: A consumer on the orders queue switches to receive-and-delete to save the settling call, and it crashes halfway through an order. What happens to that order?
hint: Lesson 20. When the message leaves the queue in that mode.

choices.text: It comes back when the lock runs out, with its count raised
choices.why: That is peek-lock; in this mode there is no lock to run out.

choices.text: It goes to the dead-letter subqueue with the reason Crashed
choices.why: Nothing is moved aside; the message no longer exists anywhere.

choices.text: Duplicate detection resends it from its window
choices.why: Duplicate detection only drops repeats; it never resends anything.

choices.text: It is lost: the message was removed the moment it was sent to the consumer
choices.why: Right. At-most-once processing, fit for data worthless a minute later and not for a paid order.

prompt: A new service starts sending the steps of orders to the queue order-steps, declared with RequiresSession, and sets no session id. What happens?
hint: Lesson 20. Once sessions are on, they are on for everybody.

choices.text: Its sends are refused
choices.why: Right. On a session queue a message without a session id is refused, so every sender has to use them.

choices.text: Its messages are accepted and given a session of their own
choices.why: Nothing invents a session id for a sender.

choices.text: Its messages are accepted and delivered in arrival order
choices.why: Without a session id the message does not get in at all.

choices.text: Its messages are dead-lettered with MaxDeliveryCountExceeded
choices.why: That reason is for a message delivered too often, not one that was never accepted.

prompt: A worker received an order, lost its connection while charging the card, reconnected and tried to complete the message. The complete fails. What does the documentation advise?
hint: Lesson 20. A lock belongs to the connection that holds it.

choices.text: Retry the complete until it succeeds
choices.why: The lock was lost with the connection, so settling again cannot succeed.

choices.text: Receive it again instead of retrying the settlement
choices.why: Right. The documented answer is a new receive; idempotence makes the second copy safe.

choices.text: Dead-letter it, since a failed settlement means the message is bad
choices.why: Nothing is wrong with the message; the connection was.

choices.text: Raise the lock duration past five minutes so it cannot be lost
choices.why: Five minutes is the maximum, and a lock is lost with its connection however long it is.

prompt: The big-orders subscription's webhook starts answering 401 after somebody rotates its key. What does Event Grid do about the next event?
hint: Lesson 20. Some answers are not worth retrying.

choices.text: Retries it on the schedule for up to 24 hours, then drops it
choices.why: A 401 is one of the answers Event Grid does not retry for a webhook.

choices.text: Holds it in the topic until the endpoint answers 200
choices.why: Event Grid holds nothing for anybody to collect.

choices.text: Does not retry it, because trying again cannot help a 401
choices.why: Right. For a webhook, 400, 401, 403 and 413 are not retried.

choices.text: Sends the validation handshake again before every delivery
choices.why: The handshake is done once when the subscription is created, not on each event.

prompt: A Python service on Flex Consumption takes 120 requests a second at its peak, each lasting 250 ms, with the default HTTP concurrency. How many instances does the peak occupy?
hint: Lesson 21. Requests in flight are the rate times the duration, and the default is one per instance.

prompt: A team sizes the internal tool from its monthly volume, 59.13 million requests, which averages 22.5 a second. What has the average hidden?
hint: Lesson 21. Two of the four numbers read off a profile.

choices.text: The duration of a request, which the volume already contains
choices.why: The volume counts requests, not how long each runs; but the duration is not what the average hid here.

choices.text: Nothing: for a fixed column the average is all that matters
choices.why: A fixed number of machines still has to be sized for the peak.

choices.text: The free grants, which the average spends first
choices.why: Grants are subscription allowances; they are not in a profile at all.

choices.text: The peak of 60 a second and the 15 silent hours a day
choices.why: Right. Those are the two numbers that decide between the options.

prompt: The office tool runs on Container Apps with a minimum of two replicas. An outside uptime monitor calls it once a minute all night. What does that do to the night's bill?
hint: Lesson 21. What a replica must not do to count as idle.

choices.text: Nothing: one request a minute is too little to leave the idle rate
choices.why: A replica is idle only while it handles no request at all; the trickle keeps it active.

choices.text: It scales the app to zero between calls, so the night costs nothing
choices.why: The minimum of two keeps both replicas, and the calls would stop a scale to zero anyway.

choices.text: It adds a request charge large enough to double the bill
choices.why: 1,440 calls a night are a rounding error in the request charge; the rate the replicas pay is what moves.

choices.text: It keeps the replicas on the active rate through hours that could have been idle
choices.why: Right. Idle means no request, under 0.01 of a core and under 1,000 bytes a second.

prompt: An endpoint of the shop builds a file while the browser waits, and takes about 235 seconds. Where can it stay a page that waits, by the limits the lesson read?
hint: Lesson 21. Three request limits: Functions, App Service and Container Apps' ingress.

choices.text: On Functions, if its timeout is raised to an hour
choices.why: An HTTP function has 230 seconds to answer, whatever its timeout says.

choices.text: On App Service, with Always On
choices.why: Plan for the same 230 seconds on a web app; Always On keeps the app loaded and changes no limit.

choices.text: Behind Container Apps' ingress, which allows 240 seconds
choices.why: Right. Five seconds of margin, though, is a reason to make it a job anyway.

choices.text: Nowhere in Azure: every service cuts a request at 230 seconds
choices.why: Container Apps' ingress gives 240, and a virtual machine sets no such limit.

prompt: By Microsoft's documentation on HTTP concurrency for Flex Consumption, a Python function app handles one HTTP request per ___ at a time by default, so six requests in flight occupy six of them.
hint: Lesson 21. Not per process inside one machine.

prompt: A compute savings plan is a fixed spend per hour across several services. Which of these does Microsoft's list, as the lesson read it, put under one? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 22. Of Functions' plans, only one is on the list.

choices.text: Virtual machines
choices.why: Right. They are on the list, as they are for a reservation.

choices.text: Container Apps
choices.why: Right. Container Apps is among the services a compute savings plan applies to.

choices.text: Functions on Flex Consumption
choices.why: Of Functions' plans only Premium is on the list.

choices.text: App Service
choices.why: Right. App Service is on the list.

choices.text: Logic Apps
choices.why: Logic Apps is not on the list at all.

prompt: The shop moves its Container App to another provider to cut its compute bill, and leaves the orders database in brazilsouth for now. What has it done to itself?
hint: Lesson 22. Which kind of lock-in belongs to the storage rather than to the compute.

choices.text: Every query now crosses the internet, slower and billed by the gigabyte on its way out of Azure
choices.why: Right. The compute decides how close the code has to stay to the data.

choices.text: Nothing: the database weighs the same whoever reads it
choices.why: It weighs the same, and the distance to it is now the internet.

choices.text: It has removed its data lock-in, since the app is gone
choices.why: The data stayed, and so did its weight; only the code moved.

choices.text: Its identity lock-in is solved, because the new provider's tokens work with Entra
choices.why: Each connection Entra vouched for has to be vouched for by something else now.

prompt: The shop speaks to Service Bus through AMQP 1.0, an ISO and IEC standard. If the queue moves to another broker one day, what stays behind?
hint: Lesson 22. The protocol is the seam; the features above it are the broker's.

choices.text: Nothing: any AMQP 1.0 broker runs the same code unchanged
choices.why: The protocol travels, and what the code uses above it does not.

choices.text: Sessions, dead-lettering and the client library
choices.why: Right. Then the day the queue moves, one function such as send_export_request changes.

choices.text: The messages themselves, which AMQP cannot carry across
choices.why: Moving data is its own line of the estimate; the question is about the code.

choices.text: Only the connection string
choices.why: Sessions, dead-lettering and the client library are more than a string.

prompt: Which of these choices deserves an architecture decision record, by the lesson's test?
hint: Lesson 22. Write one when the decision would be expensive to reverse.

choices.text: Which JSON library the export module uses
choices.why: A choice inside one module can be replaced in an afternoon.

choices.text: The name of a variable in compare.py
choices.why: Nothing about it is expensive to reverse.

choices.text: Signing a three-year savings plan
choices.why: Right. A commitment of a year or more is on the lesson's list, with a compute platform, a database and an identity model.

choices.text: The colour of the admin site's buttons
choices.why: A change there costs minutes, which is the opposite of what a record is for.
